concept.technique_name: digit-grouping column addition for multiplication by 1111

examples.problem_statement: Using the Multiplication Techniques technique: A Vedic Mathematics technique for multiplying 2172 by 1111 using a digit-grouping and column addition method. Given: multiplicand = 2172; multiplier = 1111; product = 2413092; group size = 4; intermediate steps = 7; intermediate sequence = 2, 3, 10, 12, 10, 9, 2. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: Write 2172 with leading zeros as 0 0 2 1 7 2 and set the multiplier 1111 to mean 'sum four consecutive digits'
solution.result: a digit strip ready for overlapping groups of four
solution.description: Because every digit of 1111 is a 1, each column of the product is just the sum of four consecutive digits of the multiplicand; pad with zeros so every window has four entries.
Take the rightmost window of four digits and add them; this gives the units column of the raw sequence.
Shift the window one digit to the left and add the four digits it now covers to get the next column.
Shift left again and add; this column exceeds 9, which will need a carry later.
Shift left again and add the four digits now inside the window, giving the next raw column value.
Shift left past the leading digit of the multiplicand and add the four digits covered, using zeros where digits have run out.
Shift left once more and add; only two real digits remain inside the window.
Shift left a final time; only the leading digit 2 is still inside the window, so the last raw column is 2.

solution.operation: Write the seven column values in order from left to right
solution.description: Collect the seven window sums into the intermediate sequence before any carrying is done.

solution.operation: Carry from the right: 10 \to 0 carry 1, so 12 becomes 13
solution.description: Start the carry-over pass at the right end: reduce the first two-digit column to its units digit and push the carry into the column on its left.

solution.operation: 13 \to 3 carry 1, so the 10 on its left becomes 11
solution.description: Continue leftwards with the same rule on the column just increased by the previous carry.

solution.operation: 11 \to 1 carry 1, so the 3 on its left becomes 4
solution.description: Apply the carry rule to the last two-digit column; every column is now a single digit.

solution.operation: Read the adjusted sequence as one number
solution.description: String the single-digit columns together from left to right to read off the product.

key_reminders: Multiplying by 1111 means each column of the product is the sum of four consecutive digits of the multiplicand.
Pad the multiplicand with leading and trailing zeros so every sliding window holds exactly four digits.
Carry-over is done only after all seven column sums are written, working from right to left.
common_mistakes: Stopping the carry pass after one column: here the carry cascades, turning 12 into 13, then 10 into 11, then 3 into 4.
Reading the raw sequence 2 | 3 | 10 | 12 | 10 | 9 | 2 as the answer because it already has seven entries, without reducing the two-digit columns.

concept.technique_name: speed from distance and time, then distance covered in the winner's time

examples.problem_statement:
Vinay runs 100 metres in 20 seconds and Ajay runs the same distance in 25 seconds. By what distance will Vinay beat Ajay in a hundred metre race?
(a) 10 m  (b) 20 m  (c) 25 m  (d) 12 m

solution.description: Divide the race distance by Vinay's time to convert his performance into a speed.
Do the same division for Ajay so both runners are expressed in metres per second.
Fix the clock reading at the moment the race ends: it ends when the faster runner, Vinay, crosses the line.

solution.result: Ajay has covered 80 m at that moment
solution.description: Multiply Ajay's speed by the 20 seconds available to find how far he has run when Vinay finishes.
Subtract Ajay's covered distance from the full 100 m; the remaining gap is the beating distance.

key_reminders: Speed = distance / time, applied separately to each runner.
A 'beats by distance' answer is measured at the instant the winner finishes, not at the loser's finish.
Distance covered in that instant = loser's speed multiplied by the winner's time.
common_mistakes: Converting the 5-second time gap into distance with the wrong runner's speed (5 \times 5 = 25) and picking option (c).
Using Ajay's 25 seconds instead of Vinay's 20 seconds as the time window, which makes Ajay finish and the gap vanish.

examples.problem_statement: If the salary of a worker is first decreased by 20% and then increased by 10%. What is the percentage effect on his salary?

solution.result: the single-shot formula for one increase combined with one decrease
solution.description: Recall the Quicker Maths formula that collapses a successive increase and decrease into one net percentage.
Read the two percentage changes out of the problem and label which one is the increase and which the decrease.
Put the labelled values into the formula, keeping the product term over 100.
Evaluate the expression: the product term is 2, and the arithmetic gives a net figure of -12 per cent.
Read the sign of the result: negative means the net effect is a fall, so the salary ends 12 per cent lower.

key_reminders: Net effect of one increase and one decrease = increase - decrease - (increase x decrease)/100.
A negative net percentage means an overall decrease; a positive one means an overall increase.
The order of the increase and the decrease does not change the net effect.
common_mistakes: Dropping the correction term and reporting 10 - 20 = -10, i.e. a 10% decrease instead of 12%.
Entering the values by order of occurrence rather than by role, so the decrease of 20 is placed in the increase slot and the sign of the answer flips.
